Chip Somodevilla / Getty Images A Dutch addiction and mental health institute that tests pills for users to prevent overdoses issued a “Red Alert” for “ecstasy” pills shaped like President Donald Trump’s head. The pills are actually not even ecstasy—they contain a chemical called para-methoxymethamfetamine, or PMMA for short, while ecstasy’s active ingredient is MDMA. PMMA takes longer, which the institute said could cause people to double up, thinking it didn’t work. That potential mistake would lead to overheating or even death, according to an Instagram post by the Trimbos Institute. Ecstasy is illegal in the Netherlands, but that doesn’t stop club and music festival-goers. The intelligence agency no longer needed the hardware for its future missions, so it sent the unused telescope to NASA . item.title: Japanese artist Yayoi Kusama dies at 97
item.description:
Years before the polka-dotted pumpkins, before the Instagrammable Infinity Mirror Rooms, Yayoi Kusama made art that was charged with oppositional energy. Her performances, in which she painted dots onto the naked bodies of her collaborators, were an expression of ’60s counterculture. They were protests against the Vietnam War, rebukes to the art market. Her Accumulations—soft sculptures of furniture or common household items covered in stuffed, handsewn penis shapes—were hilarious critiques of phallocentrism and early examples of feminist art. Kusama was, in other words, part of the artistic avant-garde. Her death, at 97, is a cold reminder that the avant-garde no longer exists. You could point to Andy Warhol, Jeff Koons, Takashi Murakami, or Keith Haring, but in many ways, no one epitomizes the collapse of the avant-garde more vividly than Kusama.
